docs.title: Getting Around
docs.text: Once you know a few patterns, every screen in Blossom works the same way.

docs.title: The sidebar
docs.text:
Everything is reached from the left sidebar, grouped by what you're doing:

Group Items Overview Dashboard · Beds · Map · Calendar · Weather Operations Applications · Tests · Scouting · Maintenance · Harvest · Water Records Reports

At the very bottom sit your farm name, the year, and Settings & account.

Your sidebar may be shorter than someone else's

What appears here depends on your role. If a colleague can see something you can't, that's why — the feature isn't missing, it just isn't drawn for you.

docs.title: The season
docs.text:
The year selector is at the bottom-left, beside your farm name — not at the top.

Most of Blossom is organised by season: beds, pumps, scout groups, handler contracts and management units all belong to a year.

Empty screen? Check the year first

It's the single most common reason a screen looks blank. Before concluding something has been lost, look at the year in the bottom-left corner.

docs.title: Switching farms
docs.text: If you work across more than one farm, tap the farm name at the bottom-left to switch. The year stays where it is.

docs.title: Patterns you'll see everywhere
docs.text:
• Tabs across the top of a section split it into views — Beds has Beds, Blocks, Management Units and Vines; Water has Events, Pumps, Sprinklers and Rainfall.
  • A search box sits above most lists, and it usually searches more than the name — applications search by product, target pest, bed or applicator.
  • Filters sit beside the search box to narrow by kind or status.
  • A back arrow at the top-left of any detail page returns you to the list.

docs.title: Setting your farm up
docs.text:
Blossom doesn't walk you through setup with a wizard — you enter things in the order that makes later work easy. This is that order.

Almost all of it is per season

Beds, blocks, management units, pumps, scout groups and handler contracts all belong to a year. A new season starts empty for most of these, so expect to revisit this list each spring.

docs.title: 1. Beds, and how they're grouped
docs.text:
Start here, because everything else attaches to a bed.

  1. Create your blocks first — beds have to belong to one. Blocks & management units
  2. Add your beds. Managing your beds
  3. Set up management units if you report nutrients or file NRCS 590.

Order your blocks the way you work

Block order drives the order beds appear throughout Blossom. Arranging blocks the way your crew moves round the marsh makes every bed picker faster for the rest of the season.

docs.title: 2. The farm's own settings
docs.text:
Farm settings carries a few choices that change how the rest of Blossom behaves:

  • Growing region and farm address — the address is what your Weather is drawn for.
  • Water tracking methods — bed floods, pump events, or both.
  • Track maintenance costs — off means no cost field on service records.
  • List sort order — newest or oldest first, per list.

docs.title: 3. People
docs.text:
• Users — everyone who signs in, each with a role.
  • Licensed applicators — with certification numbers and expiry dates.
  • Mechanics — whoever services the fleet.
  • Scout groups — who scouts which beds.

docs.title: 4. The things you pick from
docs.text:
Set these up before you need them mid-job:

  • Products — pesticides, fertilizers and adjuvants.
  • Pumps — sprinkler and flooding.
  • Equipment — your machines.
  • Handler contracts — handler, crop year, pounds committed.

docs.title: 5. Then start recording
docs.text:
With that in place, day-to-day entry is mostly picking from lists rather than typing. That's the whole point of the setup.

You don't have to finish before you start

Nothing here blocks you. Add a pump the first time you record an irrigation run, or a product the first time you spray it. The list above is the order that saves the most time, not a gate.

docs.title: Reading Your Dashboard
docs.text:
The Dashboard is the first screen after you sign in, headed with your farm and season — Tidmarsh Bogs · 2026 season.

It's built to answer one question: what needs attention? Each of the three cards leads with a count, shows you the worst of it, and then tells you how much more there is rather than making you scroll through it.

docs.title: Scouting
docs.text:
Headed with how much walking has been done — 12 visits this season — and how long since the last one: Walked 34 days ago. All reports opens the section.

Then the pests found in the most recent report, biggest count first:

Speckled Green Fruitworm · 29 in 1 sweep set · SMALL_LARVA · not swept last visit

The last part is the one to read. It compares this count with the visit before: down from 34 means the pressure is easing; not swept last visit means there's nothing to compare it with, which is not the same as no change.

A closing line accounts for the rest — "3 more counted, next biggest first: Cutworms 13, Cranberry Girdler 8, Cranberry Rootworm 1."

docs.title: Soil and tissue tests
docs.text:
Headed with how much sampling exists — 150 soil · 150 tissue — and then the verdict:

8 of 12 elements outside target · 4 in range

Each element outside target gets a line:

Zinc TISSUE · 50.0 ppm · Above target · Target 15.0–30.0 ppm bed E3 · 38 of 70 · 40d ago

Reading that bottom row: bed E3 holds that reading, 38 of 70 of your tissue samples are above target for zinc, and the reading is 40 days old.

The count is the priority, not the number

One bed at 50 ppm is a bed. 38 of 70 is a fertility programme. The elements are sorted worst first, so work down from the top and stop when the counts get small.

Two footnotes sit below the list and are worth a glance:

  • 5 measured with no published range — elements Blossom tracks but has no cranberry target for, so it won't call them good or bad.
  • 80 tissue samples dated outside Aug 15 – Sep 15 — samples taken outside the standard window. They still count, but tissue values move through the season, so compare them carefully.

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text:
The most direct of the three. It names the problem plainly — "17 services on 17 machines past due" — then lists the worst offenders with how far past due each is:

Oil and filter · Sprayer 6 · due Apr 4, 2024 · Overdue 1,435 hr

Overdue is measured in meter hours, not days

A service isn't late because a date passed; it's late because the machine has run 1,435 hours beyond where the service was due. That's why meter readings matter.

The card then summarises the rest — "12 more overdue, next worst first: Sander 4, Loader 7, Sander 16 and 9 more" — so you get the shape of the problem without the whole list.

docs.title: Next seven days
docs.text:
The right-hand panel runs a week ahead from today, with two columns per day:

  • Scheduled — what's planned, or "Nothing scheduled."
  • Forecast — wind, chance of rain, and the high and low: ESE 3–9 mph · 3% · 69° / 48°.

Scheduled work is grouped by where it came from. Not on a work order: covers applications recorded directly, each labelled by kind — Pesticide: Manzate Pro-Stick. Also on this day: picks up everything else that isn't an application, such as Sprinkler Event: DRY · 17 beds.

Open the ledger jumps to Applications.

Read the two columns together

Scheduled work beside the forecast is the point of this panel — three sprays stacked on a day with a 54% chance of rain is exactly what you want to notice on a Monday morning rather than on the day.

docs.title: If a card looks empty
docs.text: Cards show recent activity, so a quiet card usually means a quiet fortnight rather than a fault. A scouting card can empty simply because the last report has aged past the window it covers.

docs.title: Tips & Shortcuts
docs.text: Small things that make Blossom quicker.

docs.title: Moving around
docs.text:
• The year is bottom-left, beside your farm name. If a screen looks empty, check it before anything else.
  • Switch farms from the same place.
  • Search does more than names. Applications search by product, target pest, bed or applicator; maintenance by machine, service, notes or work order; products by name, brand or active ingredient.
  • Filters sit beside the search box — kind, status, or "none on file".

docs.title: Entering things faster
docs.text:
• Add & Clone saves the record and opens a fresh one carrying the same details. On a spray programme running across different beds over several days, it turns a morning of typing into a few minutes. It's on the pesticide and nutrient application forms.
  • One event, many beds. Sprinkler runs, floods, sandings and applications all take a list of beds. Record the day's work once across every bed it covered rather than one record per bed — the per-bed history is built for you.
  • Leave what you don't have. Partial records are fine: enter the lab values you were given, the fields your lab reported, and move on.
  • Completed is a checkbox on most event forms. Leave it unticked for work still in progress.

docs.title: Finding gaps
docs.text:
Several screens double as checklists, which is quicker than hunting:

Screen Filter Shows you Water ▸ Sprinklers None on file Beds with no sprinkler lines recorded Tests ▸ List missing ticks Beds not yet sampled this season Scouting ▸ Reports "— none written" Visits with no summary written up Weather ▸ Frost "protection on file" Beds with no frost protection recorded

docs.title: When something looks wrong
docs.text:
1. Check the year. Most things are per season.
  2. Check your role. A missing sidebar item is usually Side Bar View, not a missing feature.
  3. Check the source, not the report. Reports are views of your records — fix the record and run the report again.

docs.title: Harvest
docs.text:
How the season is coming in. Tap Harvest in the sidebar.

Three tabs:

Tab What's there Dashboard The season at a glance Yields Barrels bed by bed, typed in by you Deliveries Loads imported from your handler

docs.title: The dashboard
docs.text:
The Dashboard tab shows, for the selected year:

  • Est. harvest — the running estimate.
  • % harvested, and how many beds that is — 0 of 150 beds, with inactive beds noted separately.
  • Total barrels brought in.
  • Barrels/acre — your running yield average.

Two ways barrels get in

Numbers come from deliveries imported from your handler, or yields you type in yourself. Both feed the same totals, and a typed yield wins — see Yields.

  • Deliveries

    Import your handler's loads.

    Open

  • Yields

    Enter or correct barrels bed by bed.

    Open

docs.title: Deliveries
docs.text:
Deliveries are the loads your handler received — and they're imported, not typed in one at a time.

Tap Harvest in the sidebar, then Deliveries.

Before harvest the tab reads "No deliveries recorded for 2026 — import the handler's file, one row per load." That's normal; it fills in once you import.

docs.title: Importing from Ocean Spray
docs.text:
1. Tap Import deliveries.
  2. In Ocean Spray's grower portal, open Delivery Data by Receipt.
  3. Select the loads you want and choose Export to CSV.
  4. Back in Blossom, tap Choose CSV file and pick the file you just downloaded.

Each row in the file is one load on one bed. A row with a 0% share is skipped, so a load split across beds comes in correctly apportioned rather than counted several times over.

Import as you go, not all at the end

Because the portal lets you select which loads to export, you can import part-way through harvest and again later. The dashboard then tracks the season as it happens instead of jumping from nothing to everything.

Check the year

Deliveries import into the season you're looking at. If a file lands in the wrong year, the year selector at the bottom-left is usually the reason.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Yields — correcting or filling in barrels by hand.
  • PUR Transfer — sending pesticide use the other way, to Ocean Spray.

docs.title: Yields
docs.text:
The Yields tab is where you set barrels for a bed by hand — to correct an import, or to record a harvest that never came through a handler file.

Tap Harvest in the sidebar, then Yields.

You get a row for every bed, with three columns:

Column What it is BED The bed YIELD (will override deliveries) What you type DELIVERY BBLS What was imported for that bed

Type a figure into Yield for any bed, then tap Save Changes.

A typed yield replaces the imported figure

The column header says it plainly — yield overrides deliveries. Whatever you type wins for that bed, and the imported barrels stop counting toward your totals.

Use it to correct a bed or fill a gap. Don't retype loads you've already imported, or you'll replace good data with an estimate.

Leave a bed blank if the import is right

An empty Yield box means "use the delivery figure." You only need to touch the beds that are actually wrong, which on most farms is a short list.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • Deliveries — importing your handler's file.

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text:
Your shop record — every machine, every service, and the people who do the work. Tap Maintenance in the sidebar.

This was called Equipment

In the old Blossom this section was Equipment, and it opened on the list of machines. V2 renames it Maintenance and opens on the work instead — machines are now a tab.

Three tabs:

Tab What's there Events Every service record across the whole fleet Equipment Your machines Mechanics The people who do the work

  • Adding Equipment

    Create a machine, set its type, and group it with others.

    Open

  • Logging Equipment Maintenance

    Record a service, its meter reading and its cost.

    Open

  • Tracking Fluids, Parts & Documents

    The rest of a machine's record.

    Open

  • Mechanics

    Add or invite the people who service your fleet.

    Open

Start on Events when you want to know what's overdue

The Dashboard's Maintenance card counts services past due and links straight in — "53 services on 53 machines past due" is a worklist, not a statistic.

docs.title: Adding Equipment
docs.text: Each machine gets a record that holds its services, parts, fluids and documents. Equipment isn't tied to a season, so you set it up once.

docs.title: Your machines
docs.text:
Tap Maintenance in the sidebar, then Equipment.

Each card shows the machine's name, make, model and year, its type, how many services it has, and its schedule — "2 Services · On schedule · Next: Annual service · Mar 1." Search by name, make, model, type or group, or use Filter.

docs.title: Creating a machine
docs.text:
1. On the Equipment tab, tap Add machine.
  2. Fill in MACHINE:
    • Name — required. Your tag or number for it, like Excavator 14.
    • Make and Model.
    • Year.
    • History Units — Hours or Miles, whichever the machine is metered in.
  3. Choose an EQUIPMENT TYPE — what the machine actually is (ATV/UTV, harvester, and so on).
  4. Attach OPERATORS if the people who run it should be on the record.
  5. Tap Create machine.

History units are a decision, not a detail

Hours or miles is the unit every future service record is logged against, so pick the one the machine's own meter shows. Changing your mind later means a history in mixed units.

docs.title: Grouping machines
docs.text:
There's no group field on the form, and that catches people out. Groups are made by dragging one machine onto another in the Machines list — as the form itself says: "The machine's group is not set here: in the Machines list, drag one machine onto another to group them. Its type — what the machine is — is chosen below."

Type and group are different things

Type is what the machine is, chosen on its own record. Group is how you choose to file machines together, made by dragging. A type comes from a list; a group is yours to invent.

docs.title: Logging Equipment Maintenance
docs.text: Every service on every machine lands in one place — the Events tab.

docs.title: The service ledger
docs.text:
Tap Maintenance in the sidebar. You land on Events, newest first. Each record shows:

  • the date
  • the mechanic, or "No mechanic on file for this record"
  • a status chip — LOGGED
  • the service performed, like Air Filter Cleaned
  • the machine it was done to
  • the meter reading at the time — 2,703 hours
  • the estimated cost
  • whether it's Completed

Search by machine, service, notes or work order, or use Filter to narrow the list.

The meter reading is the valuable bit

It's what turns a list of services into a schedule. Blossom uses it to work out what's due and to show "Next: Annual service · Mar 1" on the machine's card — so logging the reading, even roughly, is worth the extra few seconds.

docs.title: Recording a service
docs.text:
1. On the Events tab, tap New event.
  2. Choose the machine and the service performed.
  3. Enter the date, the meter reading in the machine's history units, and the estimated cost.
  4. Add the mechanic who did the work, and any notes.
  5. Save.

No cost field?

Estimated cost only appears when Track Maintenance Costs is switched on for your farm — see Changing Farm Settings.

A machine's own services are also on its record, under the Maintenance tab — see Tracking fluids, parts & documents.

docs.title: Tracking fluids, parts & documents
docs.text:
A machine's record holds more than its services. Open a machine from Maintenance ▸ Equipment and switch tabs across the top.

Tab What it holds Maintenance Services done to this machine Parts Parts it uses, or has had replaced Fluids Oils, coolants and other fluids Info Name, make, model, year, type and history units Notes Anything that doesn't fit elsewhere Uploads Photos and documents — manuals, receipts, a picture of the machine

docs.title: Parts and fluids
docs.text:
Both work the same way: open the tab and add a record. Parts track what's fitted or replaced; fluids track what the machine takes and, where it matters, how much.

Fluids earn their keep at service time

Recording the oil and filter a machine takes means whoever services it next doesn't have to look it up or guess — particularly useful on a mixed fleet where no two machines take the same thing.

docs.title: Info and uploads
docs.text:
Info holds the details you set when you created the machine; correct them here as things change. Uploads is for files that should travel with the machine — the manual, a receipt, a photo for identifying it in the yard.

One record per machine

Services, parts, fluids, notes and documents all hang off the same machine, so its full history is one tab away whenever you open it.

docs.title: Mechanics
docs.text:
The Mechanics tab is the list of people who service your fleet, so a maintenance record can say who actually did the work.

Tap Maintenance in the sidebar, then Mechanics.

Each person shows their name, company (or No company if they're your own crew) and whether they're Active. Use Search mechanics by name, company, city or state to find one.

docs.title: Adding someone
docs.text:
There are two buttons, and the difference matters:

  • Add Mechanic — create a record for someone so you can attribute work to them. They get no login.
  • Invite Mechanic — send an invitation so they can sign in to Blossom themselves and work their own job list.

Which one do you want?

Use Add Mechanic for an outside shop you send machines to — you want their name on the record, nothing more. Use Invite Mechanic for someone on your crew who should be picking up jobs in Blossom.

docs.title: Why it's worth filling in
docs.text: A service record with no mechanic reads "No mechanic on file for this record." That's fine for a one-off, but once several people touch the fleet, having the name attached is what lets you answer "who last serviced this?" without asking around.

docs.title: Map
docs.text: The Map draws your beds as shapes over satellite imagery, so you can see the farm rather than read a list of bed names. Tap Map in the sidebar.

docs.title: Four ways to colour the map
docs.text:
The Filter control at the top-left switches what the beds are showing:

View What it colours by REI Restricted-entry intervals — which beds nobody may enter yet Weather Conditions across the farm Variety A distinct colour per variety Products What's been applied

REI is the one to know about

Seeing restricted-entry at a glance, laid over the actual geography, is quicker and safer than checking application records bed by bed — especially when you're deciding where a crew can work this morning.

Variety view is the one people find useful straight away: the whole farm colour-coded by what's planted where, which is hard to hold in your head from a list.

docs.title: What beds show
docs.text: Under Beds show, choose Frost or Rain and each bed carries that reading as a chip. A bed with nothing recorded reads no data.

docs.title: Radar
docs.text:
NEXRAD radar overlays the latest weather radar. Blossom is careful about what that means: "Latest NWS composite scan, a few minutes old — not live." Useful for watching a front arrive; not something to time a spray to the minute by.

There's also a Use demo rain data toggle for trying the rain view without waiting for weather.

docs.title: Getting around the map
docs.text:
Zoom with the + / − buttons or by clicking, and re-orient with the compass — Reset bearing to north. Two buttons below it get you un-lost:

  • Find my location — centres on where you are, which is the one you want standing in a bog.
  • Centre on farm — centres on the farm, for when you've panned away.

docs.title: Where the shapes come from
docs.text:
You don't draw beds by hand — shapes come from Ocean Spray contract bogs via a shape import.

A farm with none shows exactly why:

No mapped beds for 2026. Shapes come from Ocean Spray contract bogs — run the shape import, or check that this farm's beds are matched to its contract.

That names both causes, and they need different fixes:

Cause Fix The import hasn't been run Run the shape import Beds aren't matched to the contract Check bed matching against the handler contract

Shapes belong to a season

The message names the year, and the map does too — check the year selector at the bottom-left if a season looks empty.

A bed with no boundary says so on its own record: "No mapped shape for this bed — beds are drawn from their boundary on the Map page."

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
Everything you record turns into a report. Tap Reports in the sidebar.

Two tabs: Reports — the catalogue — and Data Dashboard, which draws the same data as charts.

docs.title: The catalogue
docs.text:
Reports are grouped by the part of the farm they cover:

Group Reports Beds Bed Summary · Timeline Summary · Sprinkler Summary Nutrient Management Nutrients Summary · Nutrients Detail · (NRCS 590) Management Units · (NRCS 590) 5 Year Nutrient Management Summary · Applications Report · Applications By Bed Pest Management Pesticide Use Report · Pesticide Use By Bed Report · Trap Counts · Insect Sweep Summary · Pesticide Application Posting Harvest Harvest By Bed · Historical Bed Data · Variety Comparison · Harvest Deliveries Calendar · Harvest Timeline Equipment Estimated Machine Costs · Fluids Inventory · Parts Inventory · Service History · Maintenance Due · Meter Readings Water Sprinkler Events · Sprinkler Pump Report · Water Use Sanding Sanding Events · Annual Sanding Summary Tests Traps By Year

The reports tell you what's worth recording

If a report you want comes out thin, the fix is upstream — in what's being entered day to day. Maintenance Due is only as good as your meter readings; Nutrients Detail only as good as your fertilizer analyses.

docs.title: Data Dashboard
docs.text:
The Data Dashboard shows the same ground as charts rather than tables, with tabs for Beds, Nutrients, Pests, Harvest, Equipment, Water, Sanding, Tests and Custom, a year selector and a Customize button.

Charts include Yield by year — total barrels per season, where the current season fills in as deliveries arrive — plus Barrels per acre by variety and Barrels by bed.

Empty charts early in the season

Before harvest most of these read "Nothing to show for this season yet." That's expected — they fill as the data arrives.

  • Running a report

    Open one, set the year, print it.

    Open

  • Submitting your PUR

    Your Pesticide Use Report.

    Open

docs.title: Running a report
docs.text:
Every report works the same way.

  1. Tap Reports in the sidebar.
  2. Pick a report from the catalogue.
  3. Set the Year at the top.
  4. Tap Print to print or save it.

The report opens headed with your farm name and the season — Tidmarsh Bogs · 2026 Pesticide Use Report — so a printed copy identifies itself without anyone writing on it.

Print to PDF to keep a copy

Print goes to your printer or to a PDF, depending on what you choose in the print dialog. Saving a PDF at the end of each season gives you a fixed record, which is worth having even though Blossom keeps the data.

Reports follow the year, not today

A report shows the season selected at the top of the report — not the season you happen to be working in elsewhere. Check it before printing anything for filing.

Looking for your Pesticide Use Report? See Submitting your PUR.

docs.title: Submitting your PUR
docs.text:
Your Pesticide Use Report is the record of every pesticide application on the farm. Blossom builds it from the applications you've logged — so the cleaner those records, the less work this is.

Before you start

Make sure every pesticide application for the period is recorded, with its date, beds, products, rates and applicator. See Recording a Pesticide Application.

docs.title: Generating the report
docs.text:
1. Tap Reports in the sidebar.
  2. Under Pest Management, open Pesticide Use Report.
  3. Set the Year.
  4. Review the table — one row per application, with date, pesticides (including EPA registration number), adjuvants, beds, acres and notes.
  5. Tap Print to print or save it for filing.

docs.title: If something looks wrong
docs.text:
The report is a view of your applications, so corrections are made at the source rather than on the report:

Problem Fix An application is missing Add it under Applications A bed or rate is wrong Edit that application A product looks wrong Check it on the product list

Then run the report again.

docs.title: Related reports
docs.text:
Two others cover the same ground differently:

  • Pesticide Use By Bed Report — the same applications arranged by bed, which is often what a handler or auditor wants.
  • Pesticide Application Posting — the posting and REI sheet for the field.

Sending data to a handler is a different job

The PUR is your regulatory report. Sending pesticide use to Ocean Spray or Agrian is separate — see PUR Transfer.

docs.title: Scouting
docs.text:
Scouting is its own section in V2 — it used to sit inside Pest Management. Tap Scouting in the sidebar.

Three tabs, and they answer three different questions:

Tab Answers Beds What's on my beds right now? Reports What did each visit find? Trends Is pressure rising or falling?

docs.title: Beds — what's out there
docs.text:
The Beds tab groups by month — "August 2026 · 1 report · 10 beds" — and gives each scouted bed a card showing its block, acres, when it was last walked ("Aug 25 · 31 d ago"), how much work that was ("1 sweep set · 1 visit this season"), and the pests found with their counts and life stage:

Pittsville Looper 28 · LARGE_LARVA · Red Headed Flea Beetle 26 · ADULT · Gypsy Moth 11 · ADULT

Open record → takes you into that bed inside its report.

docs.title: Reports — the visit log
docs.text:
The Reports tab lists every visit: date, scout, beds covered, and whether an insect summary and disease summary were written. Filter by scout or a date range.

Use the summary columns as a checklist

A row reading "— none written" is a report nobody has written up yet. If you rely on summaries to brief the crew, that column tells you which visits are still raw counts.

  • Logging a Scouting Report

    Start a report and record what you found.

    Open

  • Scouting observations

    Sweeps, disease, weeds, plants and more, bed by bed.

    Open

  • Summaries & printouts

    Write it up and print it.

    Open

  • Traps

    Place traps and read their counts.

    Open

  • Scouts & scout groups

    Who scouts which beds.

    Open

docs.title: Scouting observations
docs.text: Inside a report, open a bed to record what was found there. Each kind of observation is its own section — add as many as you need.

docs.title: Insect sweeps
docs.text:
The main one. Record:

  • Location — external or internal
  • Pests — each pest found, with its count
  • Notes

Counts roll up into the bed's card on the Beds tab and into the report's sweep grid, summed over that bed's sweep sets.

Life stage matters

Pests are counted by stage — ADULT, SMALL_LARVA, LARGE_LARVA. The stage is what tells you whether you're seeing the front of a flight or the tail of one, so it's worth recording accurately rather than lumping everything together.

docs.title: Plant observations
docs.text:
• Location — external or internal
  • Stages — every stage present: tight bud, bud swell, cabbagehead, bud break, bud elongation, roughneck, hook, bloom, fruit
  • Upright growth (inches)

docs.title: Disease, weeds and bee activity
docs.text: Each has its own section on the bed, recorded the same way — what was found, and any notes.

docs.title: Trap counts
docs.text: Traps placed on a bed appear here for reading — see Traps.

docs.title: Photos and notes
docs.text:
Attach images to a bed, and add notes for anything a number can't carry.

Record the bed while you're standing on it

Everything here hangs off a bed inside a dated report, so entering as you walk keeps counts attached to the right bed and the right day. Reconstructing a round afterwards is where beds get mixed up.

docs.title: Logging a Scouting Report
docs.text: A scouting report is one dated visit. Inside it you record what was found bed by bed, then write up the summaries.

docs.title: Starting a report
docs.text:
1. Tap Scouting in the sidebar.
  2. Tap Add Report.
  3. Enter the report header — the scout group and date, plus the field conditions: weather, vine and wind conditions, growing degree days, and ambient and soil temperature.
  4. Add the beds you scouted, then open each bed tile to record what you found — see Scouting observations.

docs.title: Reading a report
docs.text:
Open any report — from the Reports tab, or Open record → on a bed card.

The header carries the conditions the visit was made in — Sunny · Dry vines · Calm · Air 64°F — along with the date, the scout, who entered it, and counts of beds and records.

Below that, Insect sweeps lays every bed against every pest in one grid, with each bed's variety and sweep sets beside it. Blossom notes how to read it: insects counted per bed, summed over the bed's sweep sets. If you arrived from a bed card, that bed is marked (the bed you opened) so you don't lose it in a wide table.

Each cell is either a count with its life stage — 39 · Medium larva — or — not recorded.

The grid is the point

Reading down a pest's column shows where that pest is concentrated; reading across a bed's row shows everything that bed is carrying. That comparison is hard to do from a stack of paper sheets and easy here.

docs.title: The AVG row, and why blank is not zero
docs.text:
The bottom row averages each column, and the footnote under the table spells out the rule that matters:

AVG is the mean of the beds with a count in that column. A blank cell is left out; a recorded 0 is counted.

Recording a zero is not the same as leaving it blank

A bed you swept and found nothing on should be recorded as 0 — that pulls the average down, which is the true picture. A bed you simply didn't sweep for that pest stays blank and is ignored. Leave a genuine zero blank and the average reads higher than the farm actually is.

docs.title: Trap counts
docs.text: If any beds on the report carry traps, a second table follows in the same shape — beds down the side, species across the top, with its own AVG row and the same rule about blanks. See Traps.

docs.title: Beds on this report
docs.text:
A list at the bottom names every bed on the visit with its variety, and Add bed lets you bring another one in if you scouted it and forgot to add it.

Session notes and Comments hold anything that doesn't fit a count. Print at the top gives you a clean copy.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Scouting observations — what you can record per bed.
  • Trends, summaries & printouts — writing it up.
  • Scouts & scout groups — who scouts which beds.

docs.title: Trends, summaries & printouts
docs.text: Counts on their own don't tell you much. Three things turn them into a decision.

docs.title: Trends — is pressure rising?
docs.text:
Tap Scouting in the sidebar, then Trends.

  1. Choose Trap counts or Sweeps.
  2. Pick the pest — Black-Headed Fireworm, Sparganothis Fruitworm, Spotted Fireworm, and so on.

You get a flight graph — a weekly average per trap — above four figures:

Figure Meaning Total caught Everything counted this season Avg per trap The average across traps Weeks recorded How many weeks have data — 3 of 4 scouted Trend Rising or falling

Show as a table swaps the graph for the numbers.

A zero and a gap mean different things

Blossom is explicit about this: each bar is that week's count averaged over every trap read for that pest. A recorded 0 is a result and is drawn as zero. A dash is a week with no reading — nobody looked, which is not the same as finding nothing.

'Weeks recorded: 3 of 4 scouted' is a data-quality warning

It's telling you the trend is built from three weeks out of four visits. A rising trend on patchy data deserves another look before you spray on it.

docs.title: Summaries
docs.text:
Inside a report, write up what the counts mean:

  • Plant Summary
  • Insect Summary
  • Weeds Summary
  • Disease Summary
  • Marsh Comparison — how beds or marshes compare this round

These are what appear in the Reports tab's summary columns, and what a grower actually reads later.

docs.title: Printing a report
docs.text: Open a report and tap Print at the top for a clean copy to print or save — useful for the crew, or to send to a handler.

docs.title: Scouts & scout groups
docs.text:
A scout group ties a scouting party to a set of beds for the season. Setting them up first makes reports faster and keeps each scout on the beds they're responsible for.

Both live in settings, not in the Scouting section itself: tap Settings & account (bottom-left) → Scouting.

docs.title: Scout groups
docs.text:
1. Open Settings & account → Scout Groups.
  2. Tap Add scout group.
  3. Pick the scouting company — your own crew (In-house) or an outside company — then the beds it covers.

Groups are per season

A new year starts empty: "No scout groups recorded for 2026." Scout groups are tied to the season, like beds and pumps, so they're set up again each year. Check the year selector before you conclude they've vanished.

docs.title: Scouts
docs.text: Individual scouts are managed alongside groups, under the same Scouting heading in settings.

docs.title: Why bother
docs.text: The scout group is what appears against every report and every trap — the Scout column on the Reports tab, and the Scout group column on the trap roster. With one group it's noise; the moment an outside company scouts some beds and your own crew scouts the rest, it's the only way to tell whose numbers you're reading.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text: Traps monitor pest pressure between visits. Placing one is a separate job from reading it, and in V2 the two live in different places.

docs.title: The trap roster
docs.text:
The roster is every trap you've placed, as a table:

Column Example Bed A4 Pest Sparganothis Fruitworm Set May 10 · 19 wks ago Scout group In-house

Filter by bed, pest, set date or scout group, and tap Add Trap to place a new one — choosing the date set, the bed, the pest it monitors, and the scout group responsible.

The roster is mid-move

The trap roster still belongs to the old Pests section and tells you so: "The trap roster is part of Pests. It isn't a tab any more — reach it from the '…' menu on any Pests page." Trap counts, meanwhile, have already moved into Scouting. Expect this to settle down; if the roster isn't where you left it, that's why.

docs.title: Reading traps
docs.text: You don't read traps from the roster. Counts are recorded as part of a scouting report — open the report, open the bed, and the bed's traps are there to record against. See Scouting observations.

docs.title: Seeing what the traps are telling you
docs.text:
The Trends tab turns those readings into a flight graph — weekly average per trap, with a rising or falling trend. That's the view worth checking before a spray decision: see Trends, summaries & printouts.

A trap with no readings is invisible in the trend

The trend only counts traps that were actually read. A trap placed in May and never checked doesn't pull the average down — it simply isn't in it. The "weeks recorded" figure is where that shows up.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Soil and tissue sampling — your lab results, stored by bed and season so you can watch levels move over time. Tap Tests in the sidebar.

The screen splits two ways:

  • Soil and Tissue — which kind of sample.
  • List and Periodic — two ways of looking at the same results.

Add sample sits at the top right whichever view you're in.

docs.title: List — bed by bed
docs.text:
List gives you a row per bed, grouped by block, with a SOIL and a TISSUE column. Each shows a tick when that bed has been sampled, the date, and the headline values:

A1 · 3.2 ac · ✓ Apr 2 · pH 4.8 · P 18 · K 43 · ✓ Aug 2 · N 1.12 · P 0.09 · K 0.65

A count at the top — 150 rows — tells you how many beds you're looking at, so you can see at a glance whether a filter is hiding anything.

Search beds by name or block, or use Filter.

The missing ticks are the point

Scanning for beds with no tick is the fastest way to find what hasn't been sampled this season — much quicker than working from the lab's paperwork.

docs.title: Periodic — element by element
docs.text:
Periodic is exactly what it sounds like: your results laid over a real periodic table, with the elements Blossom tracks lit up and the rest greyed out. Each highlighted element carries an S or T for soil or tissue, the range your farm actually measured, and a one-line verdict — Boron · S · 0.11–0.80 · 150 bogs, no published range, all inside.

Below the table sit the two that aren't elements:

  • Soil pH — your range against the published one, and how many beds fall outside it: 4.2–5.4 · 4.5–5.5 · 26 below, of 150**.
  • Organic material — your range, as a percentage.

Read the second half of the line first

The useful part is the verdict at the end. All inside means nothing needs your attention; 26 below, of 150 is a worklist. The numbers before it are just the range those bogs covered.

No published range?

Some elements have no published target for cranberry. Blossom says so rather than inventing one, and still shows where your farm's values fall so you can judge them against your own history.

  • Entering results

    Add a soil or tissue test by hand.

    Open

  • Importing from your lab

    Load the lab's file instead of typing.

    Open

docs.title: Importing test results
docs.text:
If your lab sends results as a file, import them rather than typing each one.

  1. Tap Tests in the sidebar.
  2. Choose Soil or Tissue, then start an import.
  3. Pick your laboratory from the list.
  4. Tap Choose CSV file and select the file the lab sent.

docs.title: Why it asks which lab
docs.text:
Every lab lays its file out differently — different column names, different order, sometimes different units. Telling Blossom which lab produced the file is what lets it read the columns correctly.

Labs currently recognised:

  • Agroenvirolab
  • AgroLab
  • AgSource Laboratories
  • Dairyland Laboratories
  • Rock River Laboratories
  • UW Soil & Forage Lab

Lab not listed?

Enter those results by hand, and mention the lab to Blossom support — the list is something they maintain.

Import as the results arrive

Because results are stored by bed and date, importing each batch as it comes back keeps the List view's ticks honest — and that view is only useful as a gap-finder if it's current.

docs.title: Loading old seasons
docs.text: These imports are for routine lab files. Loading a backlog of past seasons is a bigger job — see Importing & exporting your data.

docs.title: Entering Soil or Tissue Tests
docs.text:
If your lab sends a file, import it instead. This page is for typing a result in by hand.

Tap Tests in the sidebar, then Add sample.

Check the season first

Results are stored by bed and year. The year selector is at the bottom-left, beside your farm name.

docs.title: A soil test
docs.text:
Date and Bed are required. The rest follows your lab report:

Group Values Soil chemistry Soil pH · Buffer pH · Organic material % · Soluble salts (dS/m) · Total CEC Macronutrients (ppm) Phosphorus · Potassium · Calcium · Magnesium · Sulfur Micronutrients (ppm) Boron · Manganese · Zinc · Copper · Iron Base saturation (%) Base K · Base Ca · Base Mg · Base H

docs.title: A tissue test
docs.text:
Date and Bed again, then:

Group Values Macronutrients (%) Nitrogen · Phosphorus · Potassium · Magnesium · Calcium · Sulfur Micronutrients (ppm) Zinc · Manganese · Copper · Iron · Boron · Sodium · Aluminum

Watch the units — they differ

Soil macronutrients are in ppm; tissue macronutrients are in percent. A tissue potassium of 0.36 and a soil potassium of 52 are both normal figures. Copying a number into the wrong form produces a result that looks catastrophic and isn't.

docs.title: Leave what you don't have
docs.text: You don't have to fill everything in. Enter the values your lab reported and leave the rest empty — a partial result is still worth having, and Blossom will show what it has.

docs.title: Water
docs.text:
Sprinkler runs, floods, the pumps that drive them, and the rain that fell anyway. Tap Water in the sidebar.

Four tabs:

Tab What's there Events Everything you've recorded — sprinkler runs and floods Pumps Your sprinkler and flooding pumps Sprinklers Each bed and the sprinkler lines on it Rainfall Rain measured for your farm, filled in automatically

On Events you can filter to All, Sprinkler or Flooding, and search water events by date, kind, reason, product, location or notes.

docs.title: Three kinds of water event
docs.text:
Add on the Events tab offers all three:

Event What it records New sprinkler event A run — date, hours and why New bed flood Water on and off a bed, and how deep New pump event A flooding pump's run, start to end

Bed floods and pump events are two ways of measuring the same water

Which you use is a farm setting: Use bed floods (inches/acre) or Use pump events (gallons/min), under farm settings. Turn on whichever matches how you actually measure — or both.

  • Recording a Sprinkler / Irrigation Event

    Log a run — dry, frost, cooling, chemigation and the rest.

    Open

  • Recording a Flood Event

    Record a flood on and off, bed by bed.

    Open

  • Setting up your pumps

    Set pumps up once so events take a couple of taps.

    Open

  • Rainfall

    What fell, and where the numbers come from.

    Open

Sanding has moved

Sanding used to sit here with the water events. In V2 it's vine care — see Vines under Beds.

docs.title: Recording a Flood Event
docs.text: Floods get recorded with a date on, a date off and a depth — for harvest, winter protection, sanding, frost or pest management.

docs.title: Recording a flood
docs.text:
1. Tap Water in the sidebar, then Add → New bed flood.
  2. Fill in WHEN & HOW DEEP:
    • Date On — required. When the water went on.
    • Date Off — when it came off.
    • Depth of flood (inches) — required.
  3. Under BEDS, choose every bed under water.
  4. Add NOTES if there's anything to remember.
  5. Tap Add.

Record it while the water is still on

Leave Date Off empty and the flood saves as open, to be finished later. That means you can log a flood the day it goes on — while you still remember the depth — rather than waiting until it comes off and reconstructing it from memory.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Vines — if the flood was for sanding, the sanding itself is recorded there.

docs.title: Setting up your pumps
docs.text: Set your pumps up once and Blossom knows which beds each one covers, what rate it delivers, and how to turn a run into a water figure.

docs.title: Your pumps
docs.text:
1. Tap Water in the sidebar, then the Pumps tab.
  2. Filter to All, Sprinkler or Flooding.
  3. Search pumps by name, type or bed to find one.

Tap Add to create one — you pick the kind first, sprinkler or flooding, because the two capture different things.

Pumps are per season

A new year starts with none: "No pumps recorded for 2026." Check the year selector at the bottom-left before you wonder where they went.

docs.title: Sprinkler pumps
docs.text:
A sprinkler pump carries an irrigation rate — how deep it waters per hour. That rate is what turns "ran four hours" into inches of water applied.

Rule of thumb for the rate

One inch of water in eight hours is 0.125 in/hr. If you know roughly how long your system takes to put an inch on, that's your rate.

docs.title: Flooding pumps
docs.text: A flooding pump carries a gallons per minute figure and the beds it fills.

docs.title: Pump events
docs.text:
A pump event records a flooding pump's run directly, rather than the water's effect on a bed. Water ▸ Add ▸ New pump event takes a start, an end, the flooding pumps that ran, and notes.

Two ways to measure the same water

Bed floods measure in inches per acre; pump events measure in gallons per minute. Which you use is set under Water tracking methods in farm settings.

If you're coming from the old Blossom: recording a flood "by pump" isn't a shortcut on the flood form any more — it's this separate record.

docs.title: Sprinkler lines, bed by bed
docs.text:
The Sprinklers tab is a different view of the same subject — every bed and the sprinkler lines on it.

  1. Tap Water → Sprinklers.
  2. Filter to All beds, With sprinklers, or None on file.
  3. Each bed shows its block, line count and acreage — A1 · Block A · 0 lines · 3.36 ac — and says plainly when there's nothing recorded: "No sprinkler lines on file for this bed."

Use "None on file" as a checklist

Filtering to None on file gives you exactly the beds whose sprinkler setup hasn't been captured yet — a far better worklist than scrolling 500 beds looking for gaps.

docs.title: Rainfall
docs.text:
You don't record rainfall — Blossom fills it in for you from the nearest reporting weather station.

Tap Water in the sidebar, then the Rainfall tab.

docs.title: Reading the season
docs.text:
Three figures sit across the top:

  • Season to date — total rain so far this season.
  • Events this season — how many separate rainfall events that was.
  • Largest event — the biggest single event, with its dates.

Below them, every event is listed newest first. Each shows the total, how many days it spanned, and the dates — and a multi-day event also names its wettest day, so "2.22″ · 2 days · Sep 19–20 · Wettest Sep 19 · 2.08″" tells you both how much fell and when the worst of it landed.

docs.title: Where the numbers come from
docs.text:
Under the heading, Blossom names the station it's using, how far away it is, and how current the data is — for example "WARRENS 4.7 WSW, WI US · 8 km away · published through 2026-09-23."

Rain is grouped into events, not days

Consecutive wet days are gathered into one event rather than listed separately. That's usually what you want when you're thinking about whether a bed needed irrigating — but it means the event count is lower than the number of rainy days.

Check the distance before you lean on it

The station can be several kilometres away, and cranberry marshes make their own weather. If the figure looks wrong against your own gauge, the station distance shown at the top is usually the explanation.

docs.title: Recording a Sprinkler / Irrigation Event
docs.text: Every reason you run the sprinklers — irrigating in a dry spell, frost protection, cooling the vines, putting product through the lines — is recorded the same way.

docs.title: Recording a run
docs.text:
1. Tap Water in the sidebar, then Add → New sprinkler event.
  2. Fill in WHEN & WHY:
    • Date — required.
    • Duration (hours) — required. How long the run lasted.
    • Reason — required, and ⚠️ pre-set to DRY. Change it if the run was for anything else. Pick from:
Reason When you'd use it Dry Ordinary irrigation Frost Frost protection Cooling Cooling the vines in heat Water In Application Watering a product in after applying it Chemigation Pesticide through the irrigation system Fertigation Fertilizer through the irrigation system Other Anything else — say what in the notes
  1. Under BEDS, choose every bed that ran.
  2. ADVANCED holds start time and notes if you want them.
  3. Tap Add sprinkler event.

Reason isn't just paperwork

It's what lets you separate frost nights from dry-spell irrigation when you look back at the season — and chemigation and fertigation runs tie the water to the product that went through it.

A sprinkler run is recorded by bed

The form takes beds, not pumps. If you measure water by pump instead, that's a pump event — a different record, not a different way of entering this one.

docs.title: Weather
docs.text:
Conditions for your farm, read against the work you're deciding whether to do. Tap Weather in the sidebar.

Two tabs: Forecast and Frost.

docs.title: Right now
docs.text:
The top of the Forecast tab names the station and the time — Volk / Camp Douglas · 9:55 AM — with the current temperature beside it.

Below that, each condition comes with a reading, not just a number:

Tile What it adds Wind Speed and direction Rainfall Today's forecast total UV index What the level means for being out in it Chance of rain Highest chance across today and tonight Feels like And whether heat index or wind chill is in play Humidity How it affects drying Dew point Whether dew or fog is expected on the canopy Visibility Pressure Inches of mercury at the station Sunrise With today's sunset

The humidity and dew point tiles are spray advice

They're written for the job, not for a weather app. At 91% humidity Blossom says "very humid — spray dries slowly and stays on the leaf"; at dew point it says "air is at saturation — dew or fog on the canopy." That's the difference between a spray that works and one that doesn't, stated in the terms that matter.

See it over the bogs opens the same weather laid over your Map.

docs.title: Frost
docs.text:
The Frost tab is built around one question: do I need to protect tonight?

  • Tonight — the forecast low, a plain verdict ("No frost expected"), and the narrative forecast: "Partly cloudy, with a low around 47. Southeast wind 1 to 6 mph."
  • Nights ahead — the same verdict for each of the next several nights, with coldest this week called out.
  • Frost protection on file — how many of your beds have frost protection recorded.

'Frost protection on file' is a data check, not a forecast

A reading like 0 of 250 beds means the information hasn't been captured, not that your beds are unprotected. Worth filling in before the season turns, so the figure means something on the night you need it.

Where the location comes from — and why it might be wrong

The Frost tab names the town it's forecasting for and where that came from, and there are two possibilities:

  • "centred on 44 mapped beds" — your beds have boundaries on the Map, so the forecast is centred on the marsh itself. This is the accurate one.
  • "from the farm address" — the fallback when no bed carries a boundary.

So a forecast that looks wrong usually means one of two fixes: import your bed shapes, or correct the address in farm settings.
